items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: It’s not like the Latin jazz of Mongo Santamaria or Ray Barretto or Tito Puente.

ctx.x: Thank you very much, Monk. Thank you, thank you very much. I really appreciate that. My intention with that album was just to do something different. The reason why straight ahead, that’s the music of my passion, straight ahead jazz. So I wanted to do a straight ahead jazz album but I didn’t want to play the tunes that most of jazz players play on a

regular basis. The standards. So what I did is I took ten Cuban tunes from a Cuban era that was called the Golden Era of Cuban Music, the Golden Era of Cuban Music, and I took ten old Cuban tunes and gave to them the straight ahead jazz treatment. And also on the album I think there’s like two tunes that we played what people call Latin jazz, but the approach, it is Latin jazz but it’s not the regular Latin jazz that most people know. It’s not like the Latin jazz of Mongo Santamaria or Ray Barretto or Tito…
Is a big part of that balancing

items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: His musical associations include work with Wynton Marsalis, Freddie Hubbard, Tito Puente, and the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra.

ctx.x: Drummer Ignacio Berroa was born on July 8, 1953 in Havana. He left Cuba in 1980 during the Mariel boatlift and within a year was playing with Dizzy Gillespie. His musical associations include work with Wynton Marsalis, Freddie Hubbard, Tito Puente, and the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra.
Ignacio was interviewed via Zoom on September 24, 2021 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
